segments.title: Blackburn's Iris: a long-range reconnaissance flying boat
segments.body: The Iris receives enthusiastic praise for its appearance. Blackburn began work on the very large long-range reconnaissance flying boat in 1924. Experience with oversized aircraft structures from the Cubaroo biplane informed the project. Major J. D. Rennie designed the Iris to Air Ministry Specification R.14/24.

evidence.note: Blackburn began the Iris in 1924 under J. D. Rennie to Specification R.14/24, drawing on earlier large-aircraft experience. The garbled caption 'great kookaburra air biplane' is interpreted as the Cubaroo biplane, corroborated by the National Aerospace Library's Blackburn T4 Cubaroo plans at https://www.aviationarchives.uk/Portal/AAAI/en-GB/RecordView/Index/4182477.

segments.summary: Blackburn drew on its earlier large-aircraft work when it began the R.B.1 Iris, a very large long-range reconnaissance flying boat designed to Air Ministry Specification R.14/24.

segments.title: Three engines for a safer overwater patrol
segments.body: Three engines gave the long-range Iris a margin against forced descent at sea. It could maintain height at full load on any two. Losing one engine therefore left near-normal flight available. After losing a second, it could still keep going, although it would probably fly lower than desired.

evidence.note: The Iris's three engines reduced the risk of a forced descent: it could maintain height fully loaded on any two and continue after two failures, probably below the desired altitude.

segments.summary: The Iris used three engines to reduce the risk of a forced descent at sea. It could maintain height at full load after one engine failure and continue after losing two, though probably below the preferred altitude.

segments.title: Hull form and the difficult transition to flight
segments.body: The Iris had a plywood-covered wooden hull with a streamlined shape and a sharp two-step V-bottom. Its clean run across the water helped it reach takeoff speed quickly. Generating enough lift to become airborne required full engine power, with high fuel use and strain on the aircraft. The same need to gain speed economically applied to aircraft taking off from land. Floating and steady flight were comparatively undemanding, while takeoff and landing imposed greater strain. Shortening the transition therefore saved fuel and reduced the demands on the aircraft. The closing line praises the Iris's appearance and calls the construction of only four aircraft "cruelty".

evidence.note: The Iris's streamlined hull aided rapid, economical takeoff from water; rapid acceleration also mattered on land because prolonged full power increased fuel use and strain. Only four aircraft were built.

segments.summary: The Iris's plywood-covered wooden hull and sharp two-step V-bottom helped it accelerate cleanly on the water. A quicker takeoff reduced the time spent at full engine power, saving fuel and limiting strain on the aircraft.
